rows.note: Which pressure to feed to injury criteria. Indoors, assume anyone within about one body length of a wall facing the blast gets Pr.

sources.quoted_phrase: Three different positions, in this respect, can be differentiated
Maximum effective pressure is the highest of incident pressure, incident pressure plus dynamic pressure, or reflected pressure.

assumed_fields: 'about one body length' distance for the near-wall case

rows.note: Oblique reflection: normal (0 deg) is a safe upper bound except near 40-50 deg at high pressure and grazing angles at low pressure (up to +50 %).

sources.quoted_phrase: For small overpressures (incident pressure below 1bar) there is a maximum at higher incident angles, which can exceed the perpendicular reflected pressure by 50%.

rows.note: Ordinary windows and doors fail about 1 ms after the shock arrives, so treat them as open vents for blast propagation (no attenuation) unless blast-rated. The interior shock starts weaker than outside, then grows by reflections.

sources.locator: Chapter 2, interior blast loads (text near Figs. 2-195/2-198 in the 2005 draft)
sources.quoted_phrase: Windows and doors will fail almost immediately (approximately one millisecond) after the onset of the shock front
This interior shock is initially weaker than the incident pressure at the building's exterior.
the interior pressure will tend to get stronger due to reflections off interior building components.

to_verify: section number in the final 2008 C2 edition

rows.value: several times the average interior pressure
rows.note: Pressure jetting through an opening amplifies pressure on the inner side; no simple published factor was found.

sources.quoted_phrase: jetting effect produced by pressure passing through an opening can result in amplification of the pressures at the interior side of the opening

rows.note: A closure resisting at most 25 psf can be treated as failing instantly (frangible); glass is never fully frangible (some reflection).

sources.quoted_phrase: if a closure's resistance to outward motion is equal to or less than 25 pounds per square foot of surface area
Blast tests of glass panels have shown that a true frangible material does not exist

rows.unit: MPa (W kg TNT, V m3 free volume)
rows.note: Peak gas (quasi-static) pressure after a detonation in a closed or weakly vented room, from TM5-1300. TM5-1300 uses 2.26 and limits W/V to 0-1 kg/m3. Example: 10 kg TNT in a 300 m3 shop gives about 194 kPa; in 1000 m3 about 82 kPa. Venting reduces duration, not this peak.

sources.quoted_phrase: In the US military design manual TM5-1300 (1990), an empirical equation (10) is provided based on extensive experimental data analysis of damage effects.

rows.note: For a detonation inside a hollow clay tile or pre-engineered metal building, assume no blast reduction outside (weight factor 1). Factors for other building types are in DDESB TP-14 Table A-5 (not read).

uncovered.subject: attenuation of blast through walls and doors (transmission factors)
uncovered.why: Not found at a simplified published level. Sourced rules: ordinary doors and windows fail within about 1 ms and act as openings; concrete or masonry walls that survive block the shock (WS9 wall model); DDESB TP-14 Table A-5 (not read) gives building attenuation as charge-weight factors.
